newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore dollar falls on finance minister comment.
newsitem.headline: Singapore dollar falls on finance minister comment.

text.p: The Singapore dollar lost its footing in late afternoon trade on Wednesday as traders dumped the currency after Finance Minister Richard Hu said Singapore's exchange rate was determined by market demand.
Hu also said Singapore's competitiveness had not been hurt by the recent weakness in regional currencies.

"Our exchange rate policy should not be guided by short-term expediency considerations. We always focus on managing the exchange rate of the Singapore dollar on a trade-weighted basis with a medium-term perspective," Hu told parliament.
The currency fell to a low of around 1.4690 to the U.S. dollar against 1.4645 before Hu's comments, dealers said.
It was quoted at 1.4682/92 at 0950 GMT.

Hu said the Singapore dollar had appreciated by 13.5 percent against the Thai baht and 6.9 percent against the Indonesian rupiah but this did not pose a major threat because the composition of Singapore's exports differed considerably from Thailand and Indonesia.
"The market bought up the dollar/Sing because he said the rate is determined by market forces," a European bank dealer said.
"With this kind of statement, you would buy the (U.S.) dollar," she added.
The dealer said the U.S. dollar's spike above the 1.83 marks level in afternoon trade also spurred buying of dollar/Sing.
The U.S. dollar would now be well supported around 1.46, with its downside limited to 1.4570, she said. "I'd buy on dips to see 1.4850," she said.
A U.S. bank dealer said the Singapore dollar would come under more pressure if the U.S. dollar continued to extend its gains versus the mark.

"Compared with the rest of the regionals, the Sing has held up the best so I wouldn't be surprised if it continues to weaken a bit more," she said, adding that the Singapore dollar could soften further to 1.48.
Singapore's dollar has fallen to 30-month lows in the past week as Southeast Asian currencies came under pressure following the de facto devaluation of the baht and Philippine peso.
